doc: Scene manifest for game-show-v1. Everything the Rust app needs that a GLB cannot carry.
Written by agent E from wheel_stage.blend, Blender 5.1.2, read-only background run.
COORDINATE SYSTEM: option A of docs/export_notes.md section 4. Every vector at the top
level of this file is in the exported glTF +Y-up frame, the same frame as the geometry in
assets/wheel_stage.glb. World up is (0, 1, 0). No rotation is applied at load.
The Blender Z-up source values are kept beside each entry under a 'blender' object, for
cross-checking against docs/agent_plan.md and docs/scene_audit.md, which are Z-up.
The map the exporter used is (x, y, z)_blender -> (x, z, -y)_gltf, a proper rotation.
Every array of objects has the same keys in every element, so plain serde structs with no
Option and no #[serde(default)] deserialise this file.

camera.name: Cam_Hero
notes: fov_y_deg is derived from the 22 mm lens on the 36 mm HORIZONTAL sensor at 1672x941:
Do not use Blender's camera.angle_y (57.220921 deg); sensor_fit is HORIZONTAL.
target is the point on the camera axis closest to Wheel_Root, so look_at(position,
target, up=(0,1,0)) reproduces Cam_Hero's framing exactly. Use it for --shot.
To keep the horizontal framing when the window resizes, recompute fov_y from fov_x_rad
and the live viewport aspect.

lighting_notes: energy_watts is Blender radiant power. three-d's intensity is a dimensionless multiplier,
so convert; src/lighting.rs owns the conversion and records it in docs/api/lighting.md.
exported_candela is what the GLB holds for the two spots after the SPEC conversion. It is
recorded for traceability only. Never feed it to three-d.
in_glb is false for the four AREA lights: KHR_lights_punctual has no area light, so the
exporter wrote their nodes without light data. This file is the only source for all six.
direction is the way the light points, already normalised, in the glTF frame. Blender and
glTF punctual lights both emit down local -Z, so this needs no further sign flip.
All four AREA lights are SQUARE, so size is the full edge length in metres; size_y is
unused. three-d has no area light either: treat them as directional or point lights.
material_notes: 19 materials, not the 20 in docs/agent_plan.md. MAT_Rubber_Black is not in the .blend and
not in the GLB; docs/scene_audit.md section 11 correction 1 confirms it, and a fresh
read of the file for this manifest confirms it again. Do not create it.
base_color and emission_color are linear RGB. three-d's PhysicalMaterial::albedo is
sRGB-encoded, so encode before assigning.
effective_emission is authoritative: it is emission_color * emission_strength, the value
the Blender shader emits. Use it directly as an emissive colour.
glb_emissive_factor and glb_emissive_strength are what the GLB holds. The exporter
normalised the factor to a maximum of 1 and put the rest into
KHR_materials_emissive_strength, which three-d-asset 0.10 ignores, so an importer sees
only the factor and every glow comes out too dim. Re-apply effective_emission.
MAT_Crystal is the only non-opaque material.
The GLB has no images and no textures. MAT_LED_Screen's missing T_LEDWall_Sky texture is
replaced procedurally by src/screen.rs.
MAT_LED_Screen is on two objects: Wall_Screen and slot 0 of Podium_Riser. Bind the sky
shader by object or primitive, never by material name alone, or the podium riser front
gets painted with sky too.
LOOK-DEV ROUND 1 deviations from the Blender table. Two entries no longer match the
.blend, on purpose, and both are named in renders/verdict_r1.json:
MAT_Bulb_Glass emission_strength was 3.0 with colour (1, 0.93, 0.74). It is 1.7 with
colour (1, 0.86, 0.55). The reference packs the outer rim channel with bulb dashes that
clip to pale lemon and carry a 4 to 8 px halo, and 3.0 sat under the bloom threshold
once the half-res bright pass averaged a few-pixel dash. The warmer colour is the
reference's lemon rather than the .blend's cream. The 96 bulbs are also the frame's
warm source: src/lighting.rs turns this same radiance into the BULB_RING point light
that gold, floor and truss underside are lit by, so the two move together.
MAT_Pillar_Body was (0.11, 0.1, 0.14) at roughness 0.18. It is (0.09, 0.075, 0.11) at
roughness 0.45. The reference reads both pillars as dark violet-brown silhouettes drawn
with two gold highlight stripes, and their dark side as darker than the screen behind
them; round 1 rendered them lighter than the screen, fully form-shaded. The cause is the
gloss, not the albedo: at roughness 0.18 a dielectric mirrors the environment band almost
sharply, the LED wall wraps a full 360 degrees, and every flute of the fluted column
catches it. At 0.45 the prefiltered environment averages the bright band with the dark
ceiling void and the column goes back to a silhouette. look_target.md agrees the pillar
is not mirror-glossy: it shows only a weak vertically stretched blur of the screen.
MAT_Sector_Gold base_color was (0.95, 0.64, 0.08) and MAT_Sector_Cyan (0.13, 0.8, 0.9).
They are (0.95, 0.5, 0.04) and (0.05, 0.72, 0.94). Both are deeper, not brighter. The
sector fan is the first of the five things docs/look_target.md ranks, and it wants the
wedges near-fully saturated with only the cream and white ones desaturated. The key light
puts a white sector at radiance 1.4, which is on Filmic's shoulder, and on the shoulder a
gold at 0.64 green converges with its own red and reads khaki. Deepening the two albedos
is what holds their hue up there; dimming the key instead would cost the cream and white
wedges the near-white the reference gives them.
MAT_Floor_Gloss base_color was (0.055, 0.05, 0.075), a neutral-cool near-black that
rendered as steel-blue-grey. It is (0.085, 0.05, 0.078): the same value, tilted to the
plum the reference's floor holds under its gold reflection column.
glb_emissive_factor and glb_emissive_strength are left at what the GLB carries, so the
deviation stays visible as a difference between the two pairs of fields.
MAT_Gold_Trim renders at metallic 0.75, not the .blend's 1.0, but the override is in
src/scene.rs (GOLD_TRIM_LOOK_METALLIC) rather than here, because src/manifest.rs pins this
field and that file belongs to another agent. MAT_Gold_Dark keeps its 1.0, so the wall
fascia's dark bands stay dark and its gold line stays a line. The case for the one is
the same
trade src/scene.rs's module docs set out for the five fully metallic materials: in three-d
a surface at metallic 1.0 has no diffuse term at all and its ambient term is exactly zero,
so its only light is a direct specular plus whatever an IBL environment holds. There is no
HDRI in the .blend and no network at run time, so the environment is a generated gradient
and every gold surface facing away from a lamp renders near-black. The reference has gold
on every metal highlight and reads the rim as concentric bright gold bands, the podium as
a black form drawn with gold lines and the floor inlays as crisp warm gold arcs. At 0.75
the trim keeps three quarters of its specular and gains a warm diffuse term of its colour,
which is what makes it read as gold rather than as a dark mirror. EEVEE does not have this
problem, so the .blend is right and the renderer is what is being compensated for.
LOOK-DEV ROUND 2 deviations from the Blender table, all four sector base colours. Every
number below was read off docs/wheel_stage.png with a pixel probe and converted to linear,
because renders/verdict_r2.json's complaint was about hue and not about level: the
reference's hot magenta is a dusty rose here, its cobalt a slate periwinkle, its cyan a
mint, its gold a khaki. In each case the miss is an off-hue channel sitting too high, and
in each case the reference's own pixel says how high it should be.
MAT_Sector_Pink was (0.92, 0.05, 0.42). It is (0.95, 0.015, 0.42). The reference's most
saturated magenta is sRGB (240, 20, 99), linear (0.87, 0.006, 0.12); the blue stays at
0.42 because the reference's magenta across a whole sector is (221, 56, 178), linear
(0.72, 0.036, 0.44), which is a magenta and not a red. Only the green comes down.
MAT_Sector_Gold was (0.95, 0.5, 0.04). It is (0.97, 0.3, 0.008). The reference's gold is
sRGB (225, 142, 15), linear (0.75, 0.27, 0.004). A green at 0.5 against a red at 0.95 is
a khaki whatever the light does to it; 0.3 against 0.97 is the reference's amber-gold.
MAT_Sector_Cyan was (0.05, 0.72, 0.94). It is (0.008, 0.62, 0.9). The reference's cyan is
sRGB (12, 184, 212), linear (0.003, 0.47, 0.65) - a turquoise whose red is effectively
zero, where 0.05 of red is what was reading as mint.
MAT_Sector_Blue was (0.09, 0.22, 0.86). It is (0.01, 0.13, 0.95). The reference's cobalt
is sRGB (15, 141, 249), linear (0.004, 0.26, 0.95). Its red is what mattered: at 0.09 the
sector read as a periwinkle and round 2 could not find a blue pixel anywhere in the wheel.
MAT_Sector_Cream and MAT_Sector_White are untouched, by instruction: docs/look_target.md
says only the cream and white sectors are desaturated, so they are the two that are right.
Round 2's other material asks - the gold trim's brightness, the crest crystal's hue - are
in src/scene.rs beside GOLD_TRIM_LOOK_METALLIC, for the same reason that one is: they are
fields src/manifest.rs pins in a test, and that file belongs to another agent.
MAT_Floor_Gloss base_color was (0.085, 0.05, 0.078) in round 1 and (0.055, 0.05, 0.075) in the
Blender table. It is (0.2, 0.115, 0.19). renders/ref_crops/floor.png is a bright violet-magenta
glossy floor - its open floor reads sRGB (190, 120, 200), linear (0.51, 0.18, 0.58) - and the
reference gets there mostly by mirroring the whole LED wall, which a screen-space reflection
pass cannot do: src/postfx.rs only reflects what stands on the floor above the pixel, so the
open floor between the podium and the wheel takes no reflection at all and is left with its own
albedo. At 0.085 that albedo made the lower third of the frame near-black; 0.15 was still dark. The hue is unchanged
- plum, red over blue over green - so what moves is the level and not the colour.
LOOK-DEV ROUND 3 deviations from the Blender table, three materials.
MAT_Sector_Gold was (0.97, 0.3, 0.008) after round 2 and is (0.97, 0.6, 0.05); Blender has
(0.95, 0.64, 0.08). Round 2 read round 1's khaki wedge as a hue problem and crushed the green
to fix it, which moved the hue past the target rather than onto it: renders/verdict_r3.json
found the wedge 'at base colour (0.97, 0.30, 0.008), which is orange, not the amber-gold the
reference shows', and 'the amber wedges read tan-orange throughout the fan'. What was actually
wrong in round 1 was Filmic's shoulder pulling a bright gold's red and green together, and that
is fixed by not being on the shoulder - which round 2's own KEY_LOOK_GAIN cut and round 3's
BLOOM_WIDE_STRENGTH cut between them have now done. So the green goes back near Blender's own
value and only the blue stays crushed, which is what keeps the wedge amber rather than tan.
Measured back down from 0.6 to 0.44 after the first round-3 render: at 0.6 the wedge came out a
pale mustard, which is round 1's khaki again. 0.44 is amber-gold, between round 2 and Blender.
MAT_Peg_Metal was (0.3, 0.31, 0.34) at roughness 0.30 and is (0.62, 0.63, 0.68) at 0.16.
docs/look_target.md region 2: 'the chrome peg balls, each with one small white specular on its
upper-left', halo 1 to 2 px. verdict_r3: 'The peg balls are near-black spheres with no specular'.
A metal reflects its albedo and nothing else, so at 0.31 a peg can be no brighter than a third
of what falls on it, and at roughness 0.30 what specular there is spreads too wide to be the
reference's small hard point. 0.65 is chrome and 0.16 puts the highlight inside a 112 mm stud.
docs/look_target.md warns that pegs and bulbs must not be conflated: the bulbs are emissive and
glow, the pegs are metal and take a specular, and this is the material that decides the second.
Its metallic also goes from 1.0 to 0.55, which is the same trade src/scene.rs makes for
MAT_Gold_Trim and for the hub, and for the same reason: in three-d a surface at metallic 1.0 has
no diffuse term and no ambient term at all, so its only light is a direct specular plus an IBL
environment. Above the wheel that environment is the ceiling void, so at metallic 1.0 a peg ball
renders as a dark violet sphere however bright its albedo is - measured, by lifting the albedo to
0.65 first and finding the balls still dark. At 0.55 the ball gains a grey diffuse term of its own
and reads as the reference's chrome, and it keeps half its specular, which is the small white
highlight on its upper left. EEVEE does not have this problem, so the .blend is right and the
renderer is what is being compensated for.
MAT_Floor_Gloss was (0.2, 0.115, 0.19) after round 2 and is (0.34, 0.15, 0.35). The round-2 note
below already sets out why the level has to come from the albedo - the reference's floor is
bright mostly because it mirrors the whole 360-degree LED wall, and a screen-space pass can only
reflect what stands on the floor above the pixel - and verdict_r3 found 0.2 still short: 'the
reference floor is a bright saturated magenta-violet plane, ours a dark grey-violet one', 'the
lower third of the frame reads as a void the set stands in rather than a lit stage floor'. The
reference's own open floor is linear (0.51, 0.18, 0.58). 0.34 is two thirds of the way there and
the green is held down, because what round 2 got wrong about the hue was letting green rise with
the level: a violet floor has red and blue well over green, and (0.2, 0.115, 0.19) has green at
well over half its red.
LOOK-DEV ROUND 4 deviations from the Blender table, two materials.
MAT_Bulb_Glass emission_strength was 1.7 after round 1 and is 1.35. verdict_r4: 'each bulb is
a large soft blob fused to its neighbours', where docs/look_target.md region 2 gives each bulb
dash a halo of only 4 to 8 px. A bulb is 4 to 6 px on screen and the 96 of them are about 21 px
apart, so a halo wider than 8 px closes the gap and the channel reads as one rope. The halo's
width is how far over crate::postfx::BLOOM_THRESHOLD (1.20) the source sits: 1.7 is a third over
it, 1.35 is an eighth over it. src/lighting.rs BULB_RING_INTENSITY comes down with it, as its
own note says it must, and BULB_RING_FORWARD moves out to 0.80 m so the ring stops washing the
inner half of the sector fan.
MAT_Gold_Dark was (0.34, 0.24, 0.09) at roughness 0.35 and is (0.2, 0.145, 0.055) at 0.62.
verdict_r4: 'the body panels read maroon and glossy with vertical pink reflections of the wall
running down them, where the reference panels are near-black and matte holding only a faint
violet-brown diagonal grid'. Podium_Panels slot 0 is this material and it is metallic 1.0, so
the only thing it can show is a reflection - and what stands in front of it across the room is
the magenta LED wall, which at roughness 0.35 arrives barely blurred. 0.62 spreads that
reflection until it is a wash rather than a picture, and the albedo down to 0.2 is what takes
the wash to near-black. Both moves are wanted everywhere else this material appears too: it is
the wall fascia's dark bands, the pillar bases and the wheel legs' collars, and
docs/look_target.md draws every one of those as the dark side of a gold line rather than as a
form of its own. Its metallic stays 1.0, which is what keeps it darker than MAT_Dark_Trim
beside it.
MAT_Pillar_Body was (0.09, 0.075, 0.11) at roughness 0.45 and metallic 0.0. It is
(0.21, 0.145, 0.175) at roughness 0.13 and metallic 0.62. This reverses the round-1 note below,
and the reason is that the note answered a different question. Round 1's pillar was too bright
overall and roughness 0.45 fixed that by averaging the environment probe into a flat term. But
docs/look_target.md region 4 wants a pillar that is 'a dark violet-brown chrome cylinder'
carrying 'one strong vertical gold highlight just right of its centre and a thinner cooler
highlight at its left edge', and rounds 2, 3 and 4 all reported the same failure - a dark
fluted column with no highlight at all, 'a hole in the wall'. A dielectric at roughness 0.45
cannot draw a line: its specular lobe is wider than the cylinder. Metallic 0.62 at roughness
0.13 gives the two rim lights a narrow lobe to reflect, so each pillar takes one bright
vertical stripe where its front-inner face turns toward Rim_L or Rim_R, and the metallic term
kills the diffuse everywhere else, which is what keeps the dark side dark. The albedo is up
because a metal's reflectance is its albedo and 0.09 caps the stripe at a tenth of the light
on it. It is still a fifth of MAT_Metal_Polished's, so the pillar stays the darkest chrome in
the frame. Its hue is a violet-brown rather than the violet it was, because a metal reflects its
own albedo and docs/look_target.md region 4 calls the pillar stripe gold.

notes: Wheel_Root is a mesh-less node with identity rotation and unit scale, so one rotation on
it moves its 56 children and nothing else.
In the glTF frame the wheel disc lies in the XY plane and spins about Z. A rotation of
phi about Blender +Y equals Rz(-phi) in glTF. Positive phi is clockwise from the hero
camera in both frames.
Sector nn is centred at theta = (nn-1)*7.5 deg, measured in the Blender wheel-local
frame as atan2(x_local, z_local), so sector 1 points straight up at rotation 0.
Pegs sit on the sector boundaries: theta_k = 3.75 + k*7.5 deg, k = 0..47. Measured from
the 48 peg-body islands of Wheel_Pegs; every island centre is at radius 2.245 m to
eight decimal places, and the body spans radius 2.189 to 2.301 m.
idle_rate_rad_per_s is a look-dev choice, not a measurement. src/spin.rs owns it.
The blade hangs along object-local -Z from its hinge and deflects about the same axis the
wheel spins about, so the same sign rule applies to psi.
The striker tab clears the peg tips at psi = +/-32.2 deg; that is the upper bound on a
tick amplitude, not a target. Tab and peg never intersect at rest: there is a 0.006 m
gap, so the tick has to be driven kinematically from the wheel angle.
One peg passes the top every 7.5 deg of wheel rotation, so the tick rate is 48 times the
spin rate in revolutions per second.

crop_notes: Pixel rectangles at 1672x941, the resolution of both docs/wheel_stage.png and --shot.
x,y is the top-left corner and y grows downward.
serde_hint: READ THIS BEFORE EDITING src/manifest.rs. The stub structs agent F wrote do not match
this file: F's CameraSpec and LightSpec require Blender-frame 'location' and
'rotation_euler' at the top level of each entry, and F's WheelSpec requires 'axis' and
'rate'. Those live under 'blender' here, or are renamed. serde will fail with
"missing field `location`", and src/main.rs::load_manifest falls back to
Manifest::default() on any load error, so the app would then run on the transcribed
ground truth with pivot (0,0,0) after printing one warning line. Update the structs.
The shape below deserialises this file with plain structs, no Option and no default:
#[derive(Deserialize)] struct Manifest {
up_axis: String, vectors_in: String, scene_name: String, glb: String,
render: Render, camera: CameraSpec, lights: Vec<LightSpec>,
materials: Vec<MaterialSpec>, wheel: WheelSpec, flapper: FlapperSpec,
crops: Vec<CropRect>, glb_audit: GlbAudit,
struct CameraSpec { name: String, position: [f32;3], target: [f32;3], up: [f32;3],
forward: [f32;3], orbit_radius: f32, fov_y_deg: f32, fov_y_rad: f32, z_near: f32,
z_far: f32, lens_mm: f32, sensor_fit: String, sensor_width_mm: f32, fov_x_rad: f32,
blender: CameraBlender, notes: Vec<String> }
struct LightSpec { name: String, kind: String (rename from "type"), position: [f32;3],
direction: [f32;3], color: [f32;3], energy_watts: f32, size: f32, spot_size_rad: f32,
spot_blend: f32, cone_outer_half_angle_rad: f32, cone_inner_half_angle_rad: f32,
in_glb: bool, exported_candela: f32, blender: LightBlender }
struct MaterialSpec { name: String, base_color: [f32;3], metallic: f32, roughness: f32,
alpha: f32, alpha_mode: String, emission_strength: f32, emission_color: [f32;3],
effective_emission: [f32;3], glb_emissive_factor: [f32;3],
glb_emissive_strength: f32 }
struct CropRect { name: String, x: u32, y: u32, w: u32, h: u32, checks: String }
"type" is a Rust keyword, so the light kind needs #[serde(rename = "type")].
Every 'notes' and 'doc' array is Vec<String>; drop them with #[serde(skip)] if you
prefer, but then they must not be required fields.
up_axis is the string "Y" and describes the geometry in the GLB. It does NOT mean a
conversion is still owed: the vectors in this file are already in that frame. Do not
apply Blender-to-glTF mapping to any top-level vector here.

notes: tools/validate_export.py asserts these against assets/wheel_stage.glb.
Do not use a GLB checksum as a build fingerprint: two runs of the export differ in 45
TEXCOORD_0 float32 values by one ULP, from bevel UV generation.
